quiz.title: Unit 3 LEQ: Governing religious diversity
quiz.headline: Governing religious diversity
quiz.prompt: Evaluate the similarities and differences in how the Ottoman and Mughal Empires governed the religious diversity of their populations in the period 1500 to 1750.
quiz.instructions: Develop an argument in one organized essay. Include a thesis, contextualization, specific evidence, and historical reasoning. This is untimed practice in AP long-essay format, not a full exam simulation.
quiz.note: Original Page One practice. Rubric categories follow the structure of the College Board's AP history rubrics; scoring here is your own self-assessment, not an official score.

rubric.label: Thesis
rubric.guidance: Responds to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.

rubric.label: Contextualization
rubric.guidance: Describes a broader historical context relevant to the prompt: developments before, during, or continuing after the period.

rubric.label: Evidence
rubric.guidance: 1 point: provides at least two specific historical examples relevant to the prompt. 2 points: uses specific and relevant examples to support an argument in response to the prompt.

rubric.label: Analysis and reasoning
rubric.guidance: 1 point: uses comparison, causation, or continuity and change to frame or structure the argument. 2 points: demonstrates a complex understanding, for example by explaining multiple causes, weighing similarities and differences, or using evidence to qualify or modify the argument.

quiz.modelResponse:
Both the Ottoman and Mughal Empires grew out of Turkic and Mongol traditions of conquest and Islamic rule. After the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453 and Babur defeated the Delhi sultan at Panipat in 1526, each empire ruled large populations that did not share the ruler's faith, including Christians and Jews in the Ottoman lands and a Hindu majority in northern India.

The Ottoman and Mughal Empires were similar in practical accommodation of non-Muslims within states led by Sunni rulers, but they differed in method: the Ottomans organized religious communities into semi-self-governing groups, while the Mughals under Akbar tried to bring Hindu elites into the ruling class, though later policy shifted under Aurangzeb.

Both empires accepted that non-Muslims could practice their religions. Ottoman rulers allowed Christians and Jews to worship and to pay the jizya in exchange for protection, and in 1492 Sultan Bayezid II welcomed Jews expelled from Spain. Akbar likewise permitted Hindu worship, and in the early Mughal period non-Muslims also paid the jizya until he abolished it in 1564. In each case, rulers valued the stability and tax revenue that came from keeping diverse subjects content.

The empires differed in how they organized that diversity. The Ottomans formalized the millet system, in which Orthodox Christians, Armenians, and Jews ran their own courts and schools under religious leaders who answered to the sultan. By contrast, Akbar integrated Hindu leaders directly into the state. He married Rajput princesses, gave Rajputs high ranks in the mansabdar system, and promoted a policy of sulh-i-kul, or peace with all. Ottoman integration of non-Muslims was more through separate communities; Mughal integration was more through shared offices.

Policy also changed over time in the Mughal case. Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679 and ordered some temples destroyed, and his long wars with the Marathas, Rajputs, and Sikhs strained the empire. The Ottoman system was more stable over this period, though Ottoman rulers treated Shi'a as threats during the wars against the Safavids.

In conclusion, both empires governed religious diversity pragmatically, but the Ottomans relied on separate, self-governing communities while Akbar's Mughals integrated Hindu elites into the state, a policy later reversed with costly consequences.

modelNotes.label: Contextualization
modelNotes.text: The first paragraph describes the Turkic-Mongol origins of both empires and their conquests of Constantinople and northern India, which created religiously diverse states.

modelNotes.label: Thesis
modelNotes.text: The thesis names a similarity and a difference and states the reasons for each, so it establishes a line of reasoning.

modelNotes.label: Evidence
modelNotes.text: The jizya, Bayezid II and Spanish Jews, the millet system, Akbar's Rajput policy and sulh-i-kul, and Aurangzeb's reimposition of the jizya are specific and used to support comparison.

modelNotes.label: Analysis and reasoning
modelNotes.text: The essay is organized by points of comparison, explains why the approaches differed, and qualifies the comparison by noting that Mughal policy changed and that Ottoman tolerance had limits.

quiz.alternateModel: A different strong essay could compare the Ottoman and Safavid empires, arguing that both used religion to legitimize rule but differed because the Safavids imposed Shi'ism on a mostly Sunni population while the Ottomans governed a religiously mixed empire with formal communities.
commonErrors: Describing the Ottoman Empire, then the Mughal Empire, without comparing them directly.
Treating Akbar's policies as if they described the whole Mughal period.
Claiming that either empire practiced modern religious equality.
Using dates outside 1500 to 1750 as the main evidence.
